[i]Hacknet[/i] is described as “an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator” wherein the person playing HacknetSSthe game – you, yourself, sitting at your computer – is the closest thing to a protagonist. It presents you with a Linux-like OS, an electronica soundtrack, and a command prompt. In reality, it isn’t far removed from Kali Linux, a distribution of the open source operating system favored by security professionals and hackers alike.

Most of the game takes place inside that command prompt, where a minimalistic tutorial teaches the player how to list files in a directory, copy and remove files, and run executables. Once the basics are established, the game goes on to provide the player with tidbits of knowledge, such as how to remove traces of your presence on a compromised system, as well as in-game analogues to real-world programs that execute buffer overflow attacks, password cracks, and network mapping.

I would go so far as to recommend [i]Hacknet[/i] to anyone interested in network and information security work as a way of gauging their real interest in the field; [i]Hacknet[/i] is simply that good.

I'm a huge fan of hacking game and have been a loyal fan of Uplink and the subsequent iterations.  This little gem is a wonderful addition to the genre.  Not only is the playstyle semi-variable (you can play utilizing just the keyboard or through a mix of keyboard/UI), it's consistent between them.  All UI-related actions show up in the command prompt as if the prompt was used.

Mechanics aside, the storyline is engaging and even plausible.  I love it!  The end made me tear up a bit.  While there may be some replayability if you weren't thorough on the first pass through, you won't be upset about obtaining this game as you'll come back to it down the road and be just as engaged as before.

Should you buy this game if you're a fan of hacker games?  Yes.
Should you buy this game if you're not a fan of hacker games?  If this would be your first game into the genre, I fully recommend it.  If the cost deters you, wait for a sale.  You won't regret the purchase.

printf("Hacknet is surprising.\n");

Because command line prompts aren't supposed to be fun. They're supposed to be tedious. But somehow, speed-typing commands into a minimal UI becomes *exciting*.

There's a wonderful cyclic experience buried in the core of this game. And it works because the game does such a stellar job of methodically introducing the player to the concepts they'll need, but in a way that makes the player feel smart for finding and interpreting that introduction, then applying it. The explanations are there, but they're buried within the game itself, and require the use of the tools that the player already has to access them. 

In a world where there's a billionty games on Steam, Hacknet is a breath of fresh air, and a unique, compelling experience.
